passage:
The class group in Valencia lit up at ten at night. Someone had posted Lucia's old dance video with cruel captions, and within minutes thirty people were adding comments about her weight and her voice.
Rafael watched from his bed. His thumb hovered, but he typed nothing. If he defended her, they'd turn on him next. He felt sick and cowardly at the same time.
After twenty minutes, he closed the group. Then he opened a private chat with Lucia. "I saw what they're doing. It's cruel and it's not okay. I'm sorry I didn't say anything there."
She replied a minute later: "Thanks. I thought everyone agreed with them."
Rafael went downstairs to the kitchen, where his mother was still working. He showed her the screenshots. She read them, frowning, and said, "You did the right thing to show me." She emailed his form tutor that night, and Rafael added a short note of his own.

qa.q: What had someone posted in the class group?
qa.a: Lucia's old dance video with cruel captions.

qa.q: How did Rafael feel as he watched the comments?
qa.a: He felt sick, scared of being targeted next, and guilty for staying silent.

qa.q: Which steps helped more than staying quiet?
qa.a: Sending Lucia a supportive private message and showing the screenshots to his mother, who reported it to the form tutor that night.

qa.q: How does Lucia seem to feel before Rafael's message?
qa.a: Lucia felt isolated and hurt, believing that everyone agreed with the cruel comments.

grounding: A teen who silently watches a classmate being attacked in a group chat feels guilty and scared, then messages her privately and reports it.

Chinmay, you look like you want to break your phone. Sit with me.
When I was fifteen, in our Nashik school, a girl in my class spread a story that I'd been thrown out of my old school for cheating. Not one word of it was true. Within two days, girls stopped sitting near me. I heard whispers on the stairs.
I wanted to scream. I also wanted to spread something worse about her. I knew things.
That night I told my mother. She didn't shout. The next day she came with me to the headmistress, and together we showed my old school's leaving certificate with the conduct remark: "Excellent." That was the turning point.
The headmistress spoke to the class. I said only one thing: "I was never thrown out. Here is my certificate." I didn't say a word about the other girl.
My two real friends stayed close. The rumour died in a week. Your Sangeeta Aaji learned: facts, calm, and good friends.

On the school bus, Disha always sat at the back with her friends. Mohit, from Class 8, sat alone near the front. He was small, wore thick glasses, and hummed to himself.
"Fair game," Disha said, flicking paper balls at his head. "He's so weak. He won't even say anything." Her friends giggled.
One afternoon the bus conductor, Pramod bhaiya, stopped at the depot and asked Disha to stay behind. "Why him?" he asked.
"Because he's pathetic. He doesn't fight back."
"And what happens to someone who doesn't fight back?"
Disha felt a jolt. In her old school, she had been the small one. Girls had torn her notebooks and she hadn't fought back either. She had sworn never to be weak again.
She looked down. "I don't want to be like him," she said quietly. "Like I was."
"You're not weak if you're kind," Pramod bhaiya said. The next day, Disha sat at the back and threw nothing.

qa.a: Paper balls.

qa.q: What was Disha afraid of beneath her contempt for Mohit?

qa.q: What helped Disha challenge her story about Mohit?

In the hill school above Rumtek, the boys from Class 10 waited at the bend in the path every afternoon to take Tushar's bus money and push him into the bushes. He'd told no one. At home he said he'd fallen.
On Tuesday, Dolma ma'am, the science teacher, walked the path home early and saw it. She called out sharply, and the boys ran.

She wrote it all down, walked him to his house, and spoke to his mother on the doorstep. The next morning she went straight to the headmaster. Tushar felt embarrassed, but mostly, strangely, lighter.

grounding: A teen whose teacher notices him being bullied feels relieved and embarrassed, accepts help and gives details.

passage:
Chen had been getting shoved into lockers at his Vancouver high school since October. He never told anyone. He said the bruise on his arm was from basketball.
On Monday, Ms Soo-ah Kim, his English teacher, came round the corner just as two boys slammed him against the metal. She stopped them with one word and sent them to the office.
Then she turned to Chen. "Are you okay?"
He felt his face go hot. "It's fine. We were messing around."
"Chen, I saw what I saw. It's not your fault, and telling me isn't snitching."
He looked at the floor. Part of him wanted to keep denying it, because what if they found out he'd talked? Another part felt a huge wave of relief.
"It's been since October," he said at last. He told her the names, the places, the bruise.
Ms Kim wrote it down, walked him to the counsellor's office, and called his parents before lunch.

qa.q: When did the shoving into lockers start?
qa.a: Since October.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when Ms Kim asked if he was okay?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of being seen as a snitch, but also a huge wave of relief.

qa.q: What would you advise Chen to keep doing?
qa.a: Keep telling Ms Kim and the counsellor details if anything else happens, because speaking up is what makes it stop.

qa.q: How does Ms Kim see what happened in the corridor?
qa.a: Ms Kim sees it clearly as bullying, not messing around, and acts at once by reporting it and calling his parents.

grounding: A teen being bullied is noticed by a teacher who steps in; he feels relieved and embarrassed and gives details.
